text: Every chip or chain you've met so far — superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom — has one more property that matters as much as qubit count or coherence time: which qubits can actually talk to each other. This lesson gives you the precise tool for describing that: the connectivity graph.

A connectivity graph represents each qubit as a node. An edge between two nodes means a two-qubit gate, commonly a CNOT or CZ, can be applied directly between those two physical qubits, with no intermediate steps. If there's no edge, the hardware has no direct physical mechanism to couple those two qubits — full stop, regardless of what the circuit you want to run asks for. This graph is a property of the physical device, not of any particular circuit, and every real backend publishes one, often called a coupling map.

This is the real thing — three unit cells of IBM's heavy-hex lattice, the topology every active IBM Quantum device uses. It looks sparse compared to a dense grid, and that's deliberate: most qubits connect to just two or three neighbors, a pattern chosen specifically to reduce a frequency-collision problem where two physically close qubits with near-identical resonant frequencies leak into and interfere with each other.

Not every layout is heavy-hex. Some superconducting and neutral-atom layouts use a square grid instead, where each qubit connects to up to four neighbors — denser, but with more frequency-collision risk. A single trapped-ion chain behaves differently still: because of shared motional modes, every ion is effectively connected to every other ion in the trap. It's tempting to ask why not just wire every qubit to every other one — but for superconducting chips specifically, the number of required couplers and control lines scales roughly with the square of the qubit count, running into real limits on chip space, how many lines can route off a cooled chip, and how much crosstalk each new coupling introduces.
Next lesson: why this graph isn't just a diagram to glance at — it's the first thing that shapes whether a circuit you design can actually run as written, or has to be rewritten to fit the hardware.
